status: REVISED 2026-08-06 — rebuilt from a 4-person model to a 14-tier law/theme model, per the user's direction that thin-narrative, law-heavy books should be themed around their actual content rather than forced into a people-only roster.
notes: SCHEMA NOTE: this book introduces role:"law" alongside the existing role:"manager"/"submanager"/"named" used in people-driven books. A law entry has 'deliveredBy' (who relays it — usually Moses, purely as transmission, not a submanager relationship) and 'purpose' (WHY this law exists / what it teaches — not just what it says) instead of 'genealogy'. Aaron is kept as a full PERSON manager, not folded into a law tier, because his role in this book is personally embodied (ordained, grieves in silence, physically performs the Day of Atonement) rather than pure content-transmission — Moses, by contrast, is almost entirely 'the LORD spake unto Moses, saying' in this book, so he's treated as a deliverer note on the law tiers rather than a manager. This distinction (embodied role vs. pure transmission) is the actual test going forward for hybrid books, not a mechanical law-vs-person split. UNDERLYING THEME tying every tier together: Leviticus is placed immediately after the tabernacle is completed (Exodus 40) — a holy God now dwells in the camp's center, and the whole book teaches how a sinful, ordinary people can safely live in His presence without being destroyed by that holiness, and how that holiness is meant to shape not just ritual but everyday social and ethical life.

characters.name: Aaron

verses.note: Consecrated as high priest by Moses; offers the first sacrifices
Silent after his two elder sons are killed for offering 'strange fire' — 'And Aaron held his peace'
The Day of Atonement — enters the Most Holy Place, sends the scapegoat into the wilderness bearing the people's sins

funFacts: 'And Aaron held his peace' (Leviticus 10:3) — his entire recorded reaction to watching two of his sons die in front of him, moments after his own ordination as high priest.

Kept as a full person-manager rather than folded into the Ordination law, because unlike Moses (who mostly just relays content in this book), Aaron personally performs and is personally marked by these events.

characters.name: The Burnt Offering
characters.purpose: Wholly consumed on the altar — nothing kept back for the offerer. Teaches total, unreserved surrender/devotion to God as the starting posture for approaching a holy God at all. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: Procedure for the burnt offering, from herd, flock, or fowl depending on the offerer's means

characters.name: The Grain Offering
characters.purpose: The one bloodless offering — fine flour, oil, and frankincense. Represents the fruit of ordinary daily labor being given back to God, not just dramatic sacrifice. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: Procedure; explicitly forbids leaven or honey, requires salt — 'the salt of the covenant'

characters.name: The Peace Offering
characters.purpose: The only offering where the offerer eats part of the meat themselves, alongside the priest's portion and God's portion (the fat, burnt on the altar) — a shared meal representing restored fellowship, not just atonement. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: Procedure for peace offerings from the herd or flock

characters.name: The Sin Offering
characters.purpose: Addresses unintentional sin, with the required animal scaled to the offender's status (priest, whole congregation, ruler, or common person) — teaches that sin has real weight regardless of intent, but also that provision for it is graded to what each person can actually bring. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: Procedures for unintentional sin, by the priest, the congregation, a ruler, and a common person

characters.name: The Trespass Offering
characters.purpose: Specifically for sins involving damage or deception against God or a neighbor — requires restitution PLUS a fifth added on top, not just a sacrifice. Teaches that wronging someone isn't fixed by ritual alone; the actual harm has to be repaid. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: Restitution plus a fifth part added, then the trespass offering itself

characters.name: Clean & Unclean Animals
characters.purpose: Dietary law — animals that both chew the cud and part the hoof are clean. Functions as a constant, daily, embodied reminder that Israel is set apart from the surrounding nations, woven into something as ordinary as every meal. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: Clean and unclean land animals, water creatures, birds, and swarming things

characters.name: Purity Laws
characters.purpose: Covers childbirth, skin disease, mold in clothing/houses, and bodily discharges — the common thread is anything involving blood, death, or decay disrupting the boundary between life and death that holiness requires guarding. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: Purification after childbirth
Diagnosing and cleansing leprosy, in skin, clothing, and houses
Bodily discharges

characters.name: "Be Ye Holy" — The Holiness Code
characters.purpose: Extends holiness from ritual into ethics — sexual morality, honesty in business, care for the poor and the stranger, honoring the elderly. Explicitly grounds all of it in one repeated line: 'Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy' (19:2) — holiness isn't only what happens at the altar. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: Sexual morality laws
Broad ethical laws — 'thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself' (19:18)
Penalties for violating the preceding chapters

characters.name: Priestly Regulations & the Sacred Lamp
characters.purpose: Sets stricter purity standards for priests than for ordinary Israelites (who they may marry, physical blemish rules for service) since they mediate directly at the altar, then turns to the tabernacle's ongoing daily/weekly maintenance (the lamp, the showbread) — closing with the one narrative episode in this stretch, a real test of how the holiness laws apply even to a mixed-heritage member of the camp. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: Priestly conduct and blemish regulations
The tabernacle lamp and showbread, maintained continually
A man blasphemes during a camp fight and is stoned per the LORD's judgment — see Shelomith and her son

characters.name: The Seven Feasts
characters.purpose: A full annual calendar binding the nation's sense of time itself to God's actions — deliverance (Passover, Unleavened Bread), harvest and provision (Firstfruits, Weeks), and a run of autumn feasts (Trumpets, Atonement, Tabernacles) closing the year by re-centering the whole community on God rather than the harvest alone. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: The full feast calendar

characters.name: The Year of Jubilee
characters.purpose: Every 50th year, land returns to its original family and debt-slaves go free — a hard economic reset built into the calendar itself. Teaches that the land ultimately belongs to God ('the land is mine,' 25:23), not to whoever has accumulated it, and that no family's poverty is meant to become permanent and inherited. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: The sabbath year and the year of Jubilee

characters.name: Blessings & Curses
characters.purpose: Closes the legal core of the book by tying the WHOLE nation's future — not just individual behavior — to covenant faithfulness, with real, escalating consequences laid out either direction. Functions as the book's own built-in stakes statement. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: Blessings for obedience, escalating curses for disobedience

characters.name: Vows & Tithes
characters.purpose: Closing chapter — the valuation of vowed persons, animals, houses, and land, and the tithe. Ends the book on the theme of what's voluntarily and formally devoted to God, as a deliberate counterpart to the involuntary, required offerings that opened it in chapter 1. (Attribution: moses)

verses.note: Valuations for vows, and the tithe of the land

characters.name: Nadab

verses.note: Offers 'strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not' — 'there went out fire from the LORD, and devoured them'

funFacts: Was a full manager in the earlier 4-person draft of this book; now attached as context to Aaron's tier instead — the death itself is now framed as part of Aaron's story, not its own separate tier.

verses.note: Dies alongside Nadab, offering unauthorized fire in his censer
Told, with Ithamar, not to mourn his brothers' deaths publicly
Questioned by Moses over the sin offering, alongside Ithamar; Aaron answers for both
Same episodes as Eleazar

characters.name: Shelomith

verses.note: Named as the mother of a man who blasphemed 'the name of the LORD' in a camp fight
Her son is stoned per the LORD's judgment

funFacts: Of the tribe of Dan. Her son himself is never named — only identified by his mother's name and his Egyptian father, itself part of the episode's point (his mixed lineage is raised during the dispute that leads to the blasphemy).

genealogyLists.note: Nothing bulk to list — Leviticus names no genealogical rosters.
